title: Rupees and Paise Converter
context: Grade 3, the changing topic of the money chapter. An adult sees a number multiplied or divided by a hundred, which a worksheet drills well. What is being settled is why: a rupee is a hundred paise, so each rupee is swapped for a hundred, and the dot on a price tag marks where the hundreds stop. A child who drops the zero from a small amount of paise, who puts the dot one digit from the right, or who sets a number of rupees beside a number of paise and picks the bigger number, has not yet seen the dot as a boundary, the paise as two digits and the unit as part of the amount.

writeup.why: Change rupees and paise into paise by opening each rupee into a hundred paise, change paise into rupees and paise with the dot two digits from the right, and choose the larger of two amounts after writing both in one unit.
writeup.look: A Rupees tray in deep blue and a Paise tray in vermilion, a paise meter below them, a price tag on a small shelf at the right, the Break, Gather, Same unit and Plain figures buttons, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Rupees and Paise Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many amounts have been changed. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A plain shop shelf fills the working area. The Rupees tray stands at x 84, y 214, 300 by 330, headed Rupees in deep blue, and holds up to nine flat rupee tiles marked Rs 1 in a grid of three across. The Paise tray stands at x 596, y 214, 300 by 330, headed Paise in vermilion, and holds the paise bars that an opened tile makes, ten flat bars of ten small squares marked 10 paise, and up to nine loose paise squares. Between the trays the Break a rupee button stands at x 400, y 330, 180 by 64, and the Gather a hundred button at x 400, y 410, 180 by 64, each labelled in words. The paise meter runs along the foot at x 84, y 560, 812 by 70, marked in hundreds and climbing by a hundred for each tile opened, in vermilion, and its full count in green. The price tags hang on the shelf at the right, the first at x 920, y 230, 220 by 120 and the second at x 920, y 380, 220 by 120, each an amber price tag with its rupees in deep blue, its dot in near-black and its paise in vermilion. Tapping a tag changes it: a tag in rupees and paise drops its Rs and its dot, and a tag in paise takes its dot back two digits from the right with a 0 filled in where the paise are few. The Same unit switch stands at x 84, y 650, 190 by 60 and the Plain figures button at x 290, y 650, 190 by 60. With the switch on, the trays slide away and the two tags become two bars of one scale, one above the other from the same start line, at x 84 and y 250 and y 400, each ending in its amount, and the longer bar is ringed green. In the Plain figures view the same working is drawn as bare numbers with no trays. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the paise or the rupees of an amount into the answer slot, and a dot key that places the dot in an answer in rupees. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag and a label. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. A note is a plain flat rectangle in its own colour and a coin a plain round disc, each with its value in large near-black type, so a value is read from the number and never from the colour. Anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because an amount is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The trays and the tag show the last amount in both units, with the meter at its full count and the dot in its place.

phases.win: the meter stops, a green tag joins the rupees to the paise, and the answer slot fills
phases.does: taps the rupee tiles open one at a time, watches the meter climb by a hundred, and types the paise
phases.goal: one rupee is a hundred paise, so any number of rupees is that many hundreds of paise
phases.says: Open one rupee at a time. How many paise does each rupee hold?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a money box holds five Rs 1 coins. How many paise is that? Say it by counting in hundreds.
phases.feels: each rupee tile opening into a hundred paise and the meter climbing by a hundred
phases.hands: Cut a paper rupee strip into a hundred small squares, put a few strips and the squares in a box, and ask each pair to count the squares in two, three and four strips.
phases.tries: First rung: say how many paise one rupee holds. Second rung: open the tiles one at a time and read the meter after each. Third rung: the same task with one tile only, before more tiles are added.

wrong.screen: the tile opens into ten bars of ten paise, the meter climbs by a hundred, and the tag reads the paise as the meter's count

wrong.why: the bars are counted one by one and each looks like a single thing
wrong.move: counts the ten bars as ten paise in all
wrong.screen: each bar is lit and labelled ten paise as it is counted, so ten bars add up by tens to a hundred, and the meter agrees

phases.screen: the Rupees tray with whole rupee tiles, an empty Paise tray and the paise meter at nothing

phases.concept: Rupees into paise: multiply by a hundred

phases.win: the tag becomes a tag in paise and its figures match the meter exactly

writeup.delight: On the first phase, each rupee tile that opens makes the paise meter tick up by exactly a hundred, and when the last tile has opened the meter glows green. On the third phase, when the last hundred paise gather into a rupee, the dot drops into its place on the tag with a small bounce and the two paise digits turn vermilion.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the Rupees tray holds a few whole rupee tiles, the Paise tray is empty and the paise meter stands at nothing. On the second a price tag in rupees and paise hangs on the shelf, with a few rupee tiles and a few loose paise squares in the trays. On the third a tag in paise hangs on the shelf with the meter full and the Paise tray holding bars and loose paise. On the fourth two tags hang on the shelf, one in rupees and one in paise, with the Same unit switch off and the trays slid to the side. One thing moves, once: the first tile gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any amount in either tray, with the meter, the shortcut tag and the Same unit scale all open, and the plain figures one tap away. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on rupees into paise, rupees and paise into paise, paise into rupees and which amount is more, each as a small price or a purse.
voiceLines: Two trays and a price tag, ready for money to change places.
Open one rupee at a time. How many paise does each rupee hold?
Break the rupees first. Then add the loose paise. What do you get?
Gather every hundred paise into a rupee. What is left over, and where does the dot go?
Are both amounts in the same unit? Change one of them, then choose.
A new amount. Which unit is it in?
Free play. Open, gather and compare as you like.
Look again at the two trays. Which part is the rupees, and which part is the paise?
You changed every amount and kept the dot where it belongs.

observations.why: one rupee is a hundred paise, so every rupee adds a hundred to the count.
observations.soWhat: to change rupees into paise, multiply the rupees by a hundred.
observations.observe: Each rupee tile that opened made the paise meter climb by one hundred, and the meter stopped at a number of hundreds equal to the number of rupees.

observations.why: the rupees were changed into hundreds of paise and the loose paise were added on after them.
observations.soWhat: the shortcut works because rupees times a hundred plus paise is the whole number of paise.
observations.observe: A tag in rupees and paise lost its Rs and its dot and the figures that were left were exactly the meter's count.

observations.why: paise are always two digits, so the last two digits of a number of paise are the paise part.
observations.soWhat: count two digits from the right and put the dot there, with a zero before the dot when there are fewer than a hundred paise.
observations.observe: When ten bars were gathered into a rupee tile, the dot on the tag landed two digits from the right, and a small number of paise took a zero before the dot.

observations.why: a number of rupees and a number of paise are counted in different units, so their numbers cannot be set against each other.
observations.soWhat: change both amounts to the same unit before choosing the larger.
observations.observe: A tag in rupees and a tag in paise could not be told apart by their numbers, but as two bars of one scale the longer bar was plain.

source_tool.description: Two trays stand side by side at the left of the working area. The Rupees tray is headed in deep blue and holds flat rupee tiles, each marked Rs 1. The Paise tray is headed in vermilion and holds paise bars, each a flat bar of ten small squares marked 10 paise, and a few loose paise squares. A tap on a rupee tile opens it into ten bars, a hundred paise, and ten bars close again into one tile. A paise meter runs along the foot of the trays and climbs by a hundred as each tile opens. At the right a price tag hangs on a small shop shelf. A tag in rupees and paise drops its Rs and its dot and becomes a tag in paise, and a tag in paise takes its dot back two digits from the right, with a 0 filled in when the paise are few. A Same unit switch lays two tags along one scale as two bars, so the longer bar is the larger amount. A green Answer tag holds what the child has typed. The number pad types the digits. A Plain figures button redraws the same working as bare numbers. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many amounts have been changed.
source_tool.art_direction: A school money box shelf / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Money is drawn as plain flat shapes: a note is a rectangle in its own colour and a coin a round disc, each with its value in large near-black type. There is no portrait, no emblem, no serial number and no small print on any note or coin, because a child reads the value from the number. The notes are Rs 500, Rs 200, Rs 100, Rs 50, Rs 20 and Rs 10, and the coins Rs 20, Rs 10, Rs 5, Rs 2 and Rs 1. A note is always longer than it is tall and a coin is always round.

Real everyday things hold the money and the prices: a purse, a money box, a shop shelf with a price tag on each thing, a bill on a counter, a school fair stall. The object is the thing the child counts, pays or reads, and a bare column of figures appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

An amount is always written Rs 25.50: Rs, then the rupees, then a dot, then exactly two digits of paise. Rs 5 and 5 paise is Rs 5.05, and a single digit of paise after the dot is never written. A whole number of rupees may be written without the dot, as Rs 36, or with two zeros, as Rs 36.00.

In a column sum the dots stand in one straight line, rupees to the left of it and paise to the right, with a heading Rupees over one part and Paise over the other. A carry or a borrow of one rupee is written small above the rupees column and its hundred paise above the paise column.
A price is a tag on the thing it belongs to. A bill is a table of the thing, how many, the price of one and the cost, with a rule under the last line and the total below.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a note, a coin, an amount or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a note keeps its own colour, a coin its own metal, a purse its own leather. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag, a label and a typed answer, because the dot between them is the one mark that tells a child which part is which. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Rupees, Paise, Value, How many and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look again at the two trays. Which part is the rupees, and which part is the paise?
voice.onNext: A new amount. Which unit is it in?
voice.opening: Two trays and a price tag, ready for money to change places.
voice.onFinish: You changed every amount and kept the dot where it belongs.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Open, gather and compare as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Rupees into paise: multiply by a hundred
Rupees and paise into paise: the shortcut
Paise into rupees: two digits after the dot

placement.where: After each pair has cut a paper rupee strip into a hundred paise squares and made a few amounts with strips and loose squares, and before any rule is written on the board. The tool is what lets a rupee be opened and closed again and a price tag lose and regain its dot while the meter counts, which cut paper cannot do quickly.

answer_key.rule: Rs 1 is 100 paise. To change rupees into paise, multiply the rupees by 100, and add any loose paise. The shortcut takes away Rs and the dot. To change paise into rupees, gather every 100 paise into a rupee, count two digits from the right and put the dot there, and write Rs in front. When there are fewer than 100 paise, a 0 stands before the dot. To say which of two amounts is more, change both to the same unit first, then compare.
answer_key.wrong: The tray is shown again with its tiles opened one at a time and the paise meter climbing by a hundred at each, and the tag is redrawn step by step with the dot moving into its place. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

items.question: A child keeps seven Rs 1 coins in a money box. How many paise is that in all? Open one rupee at a time.
items.checkpoint: To change rupees into paise, multiply the rupees by 100.
items.misconception: Writing 7 paise, because the number of rupees is copied as the number of paise.

steps: Break the rupees first. 9 times 100 paise is 900 paise.
Add the loose paise. 900 paise plus 15 paise is 915 paise.
The shortcut takes away Rs and the dot, and leaves 915.
items.question: A pencil box costs Rs 9.15. How many paise is that? Break the rupees first, then add the loose paise.
items.checkpoint: Change the rupees to paise first, then add the loose paise. The shortcut drops Rs and the dot.
items.misconception: Adding the rupees to the paise without changing the rupees first, and saying 24 paise.

steps: Gather every 100 paise into a rupee. 960 paise holds 9 hundreds, which is Rs 9.
The loose paise left over are 60 paise.
Count two digits from the right and put the dot there, then write Rs in front.
items.question: A notebook costs 960 paise. Write its cost in rupees.
items.checkpoint: Count two digits from the right and put the dot there.
items.misconception: Putting the dot one digit from the right instead of two, so the paise look like a tenth.

steps: The two amounts are in different units, so change them to the same unit.
Now compare 420 paise with 410 paise. 420 is more than 410.
So Rs 4.20 is more than 410 paise.
items.answer: Rs 4.20 is more, because 420 paise is more than 410 paise
items.question: Which is more, Rs 4.20 or 410 paise?
items.checkpoint: Change both amounts to the same unit before choosing the larger one.
items.misconception: Saying 410 paise is more, because 410 is a bigger number than 4.20.

items.question: A purse has six Rs 1 coins in it. How many paise is that?
items.final_answer: 600 paise, because 6 times 100 paise is 600 paise

items.question: A ruler costs Rs 8.30. How many paise is that?
items.final_answer: 830 paise, because 8 times 100 paise is 800 paise and 800 paise plus 30 paise is 830 paise

items.question: A sweet costs 275 paise. Write its cost in rupees, with Rs and a dot.
items.final_answer: Rs 2.75, because 275 paise is 2 hundreds and 75 paise

items.question: Which is more, Rs 5 or 480 paise?
items.final_answer: Rs 5 is more, because Rs 5 is 500 paise and 500 is more than 480

items.question: A shopkeeper keeps eleven Rs 1 coins in a bowl. How many paise are in the bowl?
items.final_answer: 1100 paise, because 11 times 100 paise is 1100 paise

items.question: A kite costs Rs 14.05. How many paise is that? Mind the paise: 5 paise is written 05.
items.final_answer: 1405 paise, because 14 times 100 paise is 1400 paise and 1400 paise plus 5 paise is 1405 paise

items.question: A toy costs 705 paise and a sticker costs 9 paise. Write each cost in rupees.
items.final_answer: The toy is Rs 7.05 and the sticker is Rs 0.09, because 705 paise is Rs 7.05, and 9 paise is Rs 0.09

items.question: One child gives 4600 paise to a school fund. Another gives Rs 45.50. Who gives more?
items.final_answer: The first child, because 4600 paise is more than 4550 paise, and Rs 45.50 is 4550 paise

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: opens into ten bars of ten paise, which is a hundred paise, when tapped
opens the next whole rupee tile in the Rupees tray
closes ten bars of paise into one rupee tile
climbs by a hundred for each rupee opened and falls by a hundred for each gathered
turns from rupees and paise into paise, or from paise into rupees, when tapped
lays two tags along one scale in paise or in rupees
redraws the working as bare numbers
types the digits of an amount

teaching_notes: Give each pair a paper rupee strip cut into a hundred paise squares before the tool opens, and ask them to make a few amounts with strips and loose squares and count them as paise. Always ask which unit an amount is in before a number is read. Wait for a child to say that one rupee is a hundred paise, rather than saying it for them. Say the dot out loud as the place where the rupees stop and the paise begin, and say 5 paise as zero five whenever it is written. If a child puts the dot one digit from the right, ask how many digits the paise take. Use fresh amounts: the printed amounts are the child's to change.
generation_prompt: Build a rupee and paise converting tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A Rupees tray headed in deep blue and a Paise tray headed in vermilion stand side by side at the left of the working area. The Rupees tray holds flat rupee tiles marked Rs 1 and the Paise tray holds flat paise bars of ten small squares marked 10 paise. A tap on a rupee tile opens it into ten paise bars, a hundred paise, and ten bars close again into one tile. A paise meter below the trays climbs by a hundred for each tile opened. At the right a price tag hangs on a small shop shelf. A tag in rupees and paise drops its Rs and its dot and becomes a tag in paise, and a tag in paise takes its dot back two digits from the right, with a 0 filled in when the paise are few. A Same unit switch lays two tags along one scale as two bars. A green Answer tag holds the typed answer. The number pad types digits. A Plain figures button redraws the working as bare numbers. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of amounts changed. A note is a plain flat rectangle and a coin a plain round disc with only its value, and no rupee sign is drawn, because an amount is written Rs 25.50. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Open a rupee into a hundred paise. Gather a hundred paise into a rupee. Put the dot two digits from the right. Change both amounts to one unit before you choose.
